volumes.title: A Light in the Hedge
volumes.text:
On the Lowlands road, a mile out of Emberwick, a carrier's cart went over a rut one windy evening and something fell off the back. It rolled into the hawthorn hedge and lay there, glowing.

Russet the fox found it at moonrise. He was a young fox, proud of his nose, and his nose told him nothing useful: hot tin, lamp oil, and a faint smell of horse. He circled it twice. The thing did not run away, so he decided it was his.

He took the wire handle in his teeth and carried it home across the stubble, with his own shadow leaping about in front of him like a second, sillier fox. All night he lay awake in his den watching the small flame and wondering what it ate. A found thing, he was learning, comes with questions attached.

volumes.title: The Moths' Complaint
volumes.text:
Russet the fox had owned his lantern for three nights and had carried it everywhere. He went along the hedge by the Lowlands road with the handle in his teeth and his chin held high, and he felt very grand indeed.

He also felt hungry. Every vole in the field saw him coming from forty yards off and went below. The rabbits simply sat on the bank and watched him pass, as you might watch a parade. Only the moths came close, dozens of them, bumping against the glass and complaining that it was hot.

"You may shine," said the oldest moth, settling on his ear, "or you may sneak. I have never met anyone who managed both." Russet went supperless to bed. The next night he left the lantern at home, and caught a beetle, and thought it over.

volumes.title: Badger Trims the Wick
volumes.text:
On the fifth night the lantern began to smoke. Its flame went tall and yellow and dirty, and the glass turned black on one side. Russet the fox carried it up the bank to Old Bramble the badger, who had lived near the Lowlands road for many years and knew something about the belongings of people.

Bramble looked at it for a long while. Then, with one careful claw, he nipped the burnt end off the wick and turned the little wheel down until the flame sat small and blue-edged, like a crocus.

"It was asking for too much at once," he said. "So it got soot." He wiped the glass with a dock leaf and showed Russet the dark line where the oil stood, already lower than it had been. "A light is not a thing you have, young fox. It is a thing you keep."

volumes.title: Dormouse on the Stepping Stones
volumes.text:
Below the hedge where Russet the fox had his den, a brook ran down to join the river Ember, and seven stepping stones crossed it. On a night of thick fog Russet heard a small voice calling from the far bank. It was Pip the dormouse, who had gone over at dusk for blackberries and could no longer see the first stone, let alone the seventh.

Russet fetched his lantern, the one he had found on the road, and set it on the middle stone. The fog turned gold. Each stone showed its wet back, one after another.

Pip came across in seven careful hops and was too polite to mention that he had been rescued by a fox. He bowed, and left a blackberry on the bank. Russet ate it, which surprised them both. It was the first time the lantern had been of use to anybody.

volumes.title: The Price of a Glow
volumes.text:
Word went round the hedge that Russet the fox had a lantern and would light the stepping stones on dark nights. Russet, who was clever, saw a chance. He set a flat stone by the brook and announced the fee: one hazelnut for each crossing, payable in advance.

The creatures paid. Mice paid, and voles, and Mrs. Quill the hedgehog, who grumbled and paid twice because she was going there and back. By the end of the week Russet had a heap of hazelnuts as high as his shoulder.

He sat and looked at it. Foxes do not care for hazelnuts. He could not eat his fortune, and nobody had left him a blackberry, or said good evening, since the day the fee began. He had made himself rich in the one thing he had no use for.

volumes.title: The Night It Went Out
volumes.text:
It happened on a gusty night at the stepping stones. The lantern that Russet the fox had carried all autumn gave a small cough, shrank to a red thread, and went out. The oil was gone. He shook it, and it only rattled.

The dark came down like a sack. Russet stood very still on the bank with his heart thumping, and it was some time before he understood why he was afraid. He was a fox. He had been born into the night and had run about in it happily for a whole year before any lantern came.

But he had looked at a flame every evening since, and his eyes had grown lazy. He crept home slowly, bumping into a thistle he had known all his life. Lean on a stick long enough, Old Bramble the badger used to say, and you forget your legs.

volumes.title: Oil from the Hazel Heap
volumes.text:
Russet the fox had a lantern with no oil in it and a heap of hazelnuts he could not eat. They had sat side by side in his den for a week before Mrs. Quill the hedgehog, calling to complain about the dark at the stepping stones, looked from one to the other and sighed. "Nuts have oil in them," she said. "Anyone knows that. Fetch two flat stones."

So they pressed them. The mice cracked the shells, Pip the dormouse sorted the kernels, and Russet turned the top stone round and round until a thin gold thread ran into an acorn cup. It took three evenings to fill the lantern. Nobody mentioned the fee, and nobody was asked for one again.

The flame, when it came, smelled faintly of toast. Every creature who had once paid a nut could say truthfully that a little of that light was theirs.

volumes.title: The Owl Objects
volumes.text:
Not everyone along the Lowlands hedge loved the lantern. Mistle the owl flew down one evening and landed on the handle, which made the whole thing swing.

"I hunt by dark," she told Russet the fox. "I have done so since before you had a tail. Now there is a yellow smear in the middle of my night, and every mouse can see me against it. The dark is not an emptiness, fox. Some of us live in it."

Russet had not thought of that. He had supposed that what was good for the dormouse must be good for all. They talked until the moon set and came to terms: the lantern would burn at the stepping stones in fog and on moonless nights, and stay shuttered otherwise. Mistle got her dark back. The crossers kept their light. Neither had everything, and both slept well.

volumes.title: The Hare's Enormous Shadow
volumes.text:
A leveret named Hazel came to the stepping stones one moonless night, saw the lantern burning on the middle stone, and would not cross. Something huge and black with ears like fence posts was crouching on the far bank, she said. It moved whenever she moved.

Russet the fox, who kept the lantern, looked where she pointed. Then he lifted one paw. On the far bank a monstrous paw rose too.

"That one is mine," he said. "The long-eared one is yours. The light is behind us, so we are thrown large." He made a goose with his tail and a tree with his whole self. Hazel, after a moment, tried a rabbit, which was not difficult. They played until the oil ran low. She crossed at last, hopping straight through the place where the monster had been, and it did her no harm at all.

volumes.title: The Carrier Comes Back
volumes.text:
Late in the autumn the carrier's cart came creaking along the Lowlands road again, the same cart that had dropped the lantern months before. Russet the fox watched from the hedge. The carrier, an old man in a sacking hood, climbed down at the rut and poked about in the hawthorn with a stick.

"It was here I lost her," he told the horse. "Thirty years I had that lantern." He found nothing, of course. He drove on toward Emberwick in the dusk with no light at all, the horse feeling for the road with its feet.

Russet went home and looked at the lantern for a long time. He had trimmed it and fed it. He had earned it, surely. But he knew the smell of that hood and that horse. It had been on the tin since the first night, and he had always known what it meant.

volumes.title: A Fox at the Milestone
volumes.text:
There is a milestone on the Lowlands road that says Emberwick, one mile. On a cold evening Russet the fox carried his lantern there, the lantern he had found in the hedge and kept all autumn. He trimmed the wick as Old Bramble the badger had taught him, set it burning on top of the stone, and backed away into the bracken.

The carrier's cart came by at dusk. The old man pulled up so sharply that the horse snorted. He got down, turned the lantern round in his hands, and found it clean, full, and lit.

He looked at the hedge for some while. Then he took off his hood to it, quite seriously, as one does to a neighbour, and left half a cheese rind on the milestone. The light went swinging off down the road. Russet watched until it was the size of a star.

volumes.title: Seeing in the Dark
volumes.text:
Fog lay on the brook again, as thick as on the night Russet the fox first lit the stepping stones. A small voice called from the far bank. It was Pip the dormouse, late home, with no lantern to hope for now that it had gone back to the carrier.

Russet waded to the middle stone and stood there. His eyes, after a month of honest darkness, had come back to him. "Follow the white tip of my tail," he called. "It is the palest thing out here. Seven hops."

Pip counted them aloud and arrived safely. After that Russet stood on the middle stone whenever the fog came down, and the creatures crossed by his tail. Some evenings a small gold light went by on the Lowlands road, and a hood was raised toward the hedge, and a fox, unseen, raised his chin in reply.

volumes.title: A Room in the Roots
volumes.text:
The hollow oak stands where the Lowlands fields give way to the marsh, and it is older than the oldest hedge in Emberwick. On a night of hard autumn rain a woodmouse named Thimble came to it with everything she owned, which was a wet tail and a seed.

The marsh had risen into her burrow. She had walked since dusk. Between two roots she found a dry hollow and, sitting in it, a large toad who introduced himself as Mudge.

"There is room," he said, moving over an inch, which for a toad is generous. "There is one rule. Nobody eats anybody under these branches. Beyond the drip of the leaves, the world goes on as usual. In here, we are neighbours." Thimble agreed at once. She did not yet know who lived upstairs, or she might have asked a question or two first.

volumes.title: The Squirrel Who Counted
volumes.text:
Halfway up the hollow oak lived a squirrel named Pocket, and in autumn Pocket counted. He counted acorns into the fork of the oak, acorns into a knothole, acorns into forty small holes he dug between the roots. Three hundred and twelve, he told anyone who passed, and not one to spare.

Thimble the woodmouse, new to the tree, asked him for a single acorn against the winter. Pocket said he was very sorry. Every one was counted.

By the first frost he had forgotten where a good third of them were. He dug up the same empty hole four times and accused a jay. Old Mudge the toad, watching from the roots, remarked that a thing kept too carefully is as good as lost; but the oak, he added, would not mind. Oaks have always relied on a squirrel's poor memory.

volumes.title: The Owl Upstairs
volumes.text:
The top of the hollow oak belonged to Dame Sorrel, a tawny owl. Thimble the woodmouse, who lived among the roots, learned this on her third evening when a soft brown shape the size of a thundercloud dropped past her door without a sound.

She did not go out for two days. On the third, hunger sent her up the trunk for a beechnut lodged in the bark, and there was the owl on a branch, looking at her with eyes like two lamps.

"Good evening," said Dame Sorrel. "You are the new mouse. I hunt beyond the far hedge. It is a long flight on an empty stomach, and you look a good deal closer, but a rule is a rule." Thimble said good evening back, in a squeak. It struck her afterwards that the owl's half of the bargain was much the harder to keep.

volumes.title: The Woodpecker's Early Drum
volumes.text:
Burr the woodpecker drummed on the hollow oak at first light, every morning, on the loudest dead branch he could find. The bats, who had only just hung themselves up to sleep, sent a complaint. So did Dame Sorrel the owl. Thimble the woodmouse, down in the roots, signed it with a muddy paw.

Burr was hurt, but he stopped. The oak was beautifully quiet for a week.

It was also late for everything. Pocket the squirrel slept until noon and missed the best of the beechnuts. Thimble woke in the dark, not knowing if it was evening or morning. The bats went out too early and met a hawk. In the end a second letter went up the trunk, a politer one. Burr now gives three knocks at dawn, no more, and does the rest of his drumming at midday on the old elm across the field.

volumes.title: First Frost Supper
volumes.text:
On the night of the first frost the tenants of the hollow oak hold a supper inside the trunk, where the floor is soft with a hundred years of leaf dust. Everyone brings something. That is the custom.

Dame Sorrel the owl brought a tuft of sheep's wool for sitting on. Burr the woodpecker brought beetle grubs, which only he enjoyed. Thimble the woodmouse brought her one seed, carried all the way from the marsh, and cut it into five. Pocket the squirrel, after a long struggle, brought an acorn. One.

Mudge the toad brought nothing he could carry. He was sleepy with the cold and due under the mud until spring. Instead he told the story of the winter the snow reached the first branch, and told it well. They agreed afterwards that it had been the best dish on the table.

volumes.title: The Night of the Gale
volumes.text:
At midwinter a gale came down off the Northern Fells and leaned on the hollow oak all night. Towards morning the great west limb gave a crack like a gate slamming and fell into the field.

Nobody was hurt. But Dame Sorrel's ledge had gone with it, and Burr the woodpecker's hole, and half of Pocket the squirrel's knothole store. The three of them sat in the wreckage in the grey light, looking smaller than usual.

Thimble the woodmouse offered her root room to the owl, who thanked her gravely and did not fit. So everyone shifted. Burr took the bats' spare crack. Pocket squeezed his acorns into the fork and himself into the knothole. The owl had the whole inside of the trunk, standing up, like an umbrella in a stand. Nobody was comfortable, exactly. Everybody was indoors.

volumes.title: The Jay's Bad News
volumes.text:
After the gale a jay named Jabber stopped at the hollow oak on his way somewhere else. He looked at the fallen limb, and at the great dark hole in the trunk, and whistled.

"Hollow," he said. "Rotten right through. A hollow tree is a dead tree, friends. I would be out of it by spring. There is a nice young beech by the road." Then he flew off, having done his duty.

The oak was in an uproar by dusk. Pocket the squirrel began carrying acorns to the beech, two at a time, and losing them on the way. Thimble the woodmouse cried into her tail. Only Dame Sorrel the owl stayed where she was. "That bird," she said, "has known this tree for the length of one conversation. I should like a second opinion from somebody who lives here."

volumes.title: What the Bats Heard
volumes.text:
Was the hollow oak dying? A passing jay had said so, and the tenants had talked of little else for a week. Nobody had thought to ask the bats. Nobody ever did. They hung in a row inside the trunk all winter, eleven of them, and said nothing.

Thimble the woodmouse climbed up and asked. The oldest bat opened one eye.

"We sleep with our ears against the wood," she said. "The middle is empty, yes. It has been empty since before your grandmother. But on mild days we hear the outside drinking. Go and listen." Thimble went down and pressed her ear to the rough bark in the weak noon sun. She heard nothing for a long time. Then, very faint and very slow, came something like a river running under a floor. She called the others, one by one, to hear it.

volumes.title: Thaw and Toad
volumes.text:
The thaw came to the hollow oak in a single night. By morning the snow had gone into the ground, and a good deal of it had come out again in Thimble the woodmouse's root room, where she stood bailing with a nutshell.

A lump of mud in the corner yawned. It was Mudge the toad, awake a month early and not pleased. He listened to the winter's news: the gale, the fallen limb, the jay who said the tree was finished.

"Hollow," said Mudge. "Of course it is hollow. It was hollow when my grandfather wintered here, and he complained of the draught. Where did they suppose we all lived, in a solid tree? The hollow is the room, child." He climbed onto a root to watch the water go down. It went down by noon, as he said it would, and he went back to bed.

volumes.title: Buds on the Broken Side
volumes.text:
In April the hollow oak came into leaf, late as oaks are, and all over. There were buds even on the west side, round the pale scar where the great limb had torn away in the winter gale.

The tenants went about their repairs. Burr the woodpecker began a new hole a yard above his old one and pronounced the wood sounder there. Pocket the squirrel found the knothole pleasantly roomy now that half his acorns were eaten.

Dame Sorrel the owl had the best of it. The stump of the fallen limb had split into a deep, dry cup, sheltered from the north, with a view of the whole field. She turned round in it three times and settled. It was, she admitted to Thimble the woodmouse, a better ledge than the one she had lost; though she would not have chosen the way of getting it.

volumes.title: The Forgotten Acorn
volumes.text:
Pocket the squirrel spent a spring morning digging between the roots of the hollow oak for acorns he had buried in autumn and mislaid. He found three empty holes, a snail, and then a thing he did not expect: a red stem as long as his paw, with two crumpled leaves on top.

At the bottom of the stem, half split, sat one of his acorns. He reached for it.

"Leave it," said Thimble the woodmouse, from her doorway. "It is busy." Pocket looked at the little oak, and up at the enormous one, and down again. He did the sum slowly. Then he fetched twigs and built a fence round it against rabbits, and from that day he visited every morning to count its leaves. Two. Then four. It was the first counting he had ever done that made the number go up.

volumes.title: Another Wet Traveller
volumes.text:
Autumn came round to the hollow oak again, and with it a night of hard rain off the marsh. Thimble the woodmouse was sweeping her root room when a shrew appeared between the roots, soaked to the skin and carrying nothing at all.

"There is room," said Thimble, moving over. She heard herself say it in old Mudge's voice, and the toad, from his corner, shut one eye at her. "There is one rule. Nobody eats anybody under these branches."

She showed the shrew where the dry leaves were kept. She pointed out the little oak by the door, six leaves tall inside its fence of twigs, and explained that the squirrel would want it admired. Far overhead something soft and brown went out to hunt beyond the far hedge. "That is the owl upstairs," said Thimble. "Say good evening. She likes to be asked."

volumes.title: What the River Left
volumes.text:
When the spring flood went down, the river Ember left a number of things in the reeds below Emberwick: a boot, a gatepost, and a tin kettle lying on its side with the lid still on.

Mrs. Dabble the water vole found the kettle. The same flood had filled her burrow with silt, and she was looking for somewhere to dry her whiskers. She walked round it twice. She knocked on it, and it rang. She pushed up the lid with her nose and looked in.

It was dry inside, and round, and smelled only a little of rust. The spout pointed at the sky like a chimney. By evening she had carried in a bed of reed fluff and was sitting in the doorway, well pleased. Somebody upstream had thrown away a kettle. Somebody downstream had been given a house.

volumes.title: The First Cup of Mint
volumes.text:
Mrs. Dabble the water vole had lived in the tin kettle among the reeds for a week when she discovered what it was good at. On a sunny day the tin grew warm, and rainwater left standing in the upturned lid grew warm with it. She dropped in a sprig of water mint to see what would happen.

What happened was tea, of a kind. It was pale green and smelled like the riverbank after a shower.

Two young frogs, Plip and Plop, followed the smell to her door and stood there being obvious. Mrs. Dabble owned exactly one acorn cup. She filled it and handed it out, and the frogs passed it between them, sip and sip about, until it was empty. They came back the next day with a friend. A door that opens once, she found, is expected to open again.

volumes.title: The Heron Will Not Stoop
volumes.text:
Every creature in the marsh below Emberwick had taken a cup of mint tea at the tin kettle, except one. Grimsby the heron stood in the shallows twenty yards off, grey and narrow as a fence rail, and looked the other way.

"A kettle," he was heard to say, "is not a house. And I do not bend to doorways." He was a good deal too tall for this one, which may have been the trouble.

Mrs. Dabble the water vole did not argue. Each evening she climbed the handle and set a full acorn cup on the very top of the kettle, where a tall bird might find it without stooping an inch. For nine evenings it stood untouched and went cold. On the tenth morning the cup was empty and turned neatly upside down. Nobody said a word about it, the heron least of all.

volumes.title: Otter Takes Too Much
volumes.text:
Ripple the otter discovered the tin kettle in May. He arrived like a wave, drank the lid dry, ate eleven seed cakes, and told a story about a pike that lasted until the moon was up. The next day he did it again.

By the end of the week the frogs had stopped calling. There was no tea left for them, and no silence to put a word into. Mrs. Dabble the water vole looked at her bare shelf and at her large, cheerful guest.

She did not send him away. She gave him a rush basket. The best mint, she explained, grew a mile upstream past the weir, too far for a vole. Ripple was back within the hour, soaked and proud, with enough mint for a month. A big appetite, she had noticed, usually comes with big legs. He has been the kettle's carrier ever since.

volumes.title: The Newt Who Listened
volumes.text:
Fig the newt came to the tin kettle every evening, sat under the spout, and said nothing. The frogs thought him dull. Ripple the otter, who filled every silence he met, once asked Mrs. Dabble the water vole whether the newt was quite awake.

Then, at midsummer, the moorhen Mrs. Coot came splashing through the reeds in a terrible state. Her smallest chick was missing. Everyone talked at once and nobody knew anything.

Fig cleared his throat. It took a moment to be noticed. "On Tuesday," he said, "the chick told the frogs she wished to see the boot the flood left by the alder. Nobody answered her. I expect she has gone to look." She had. She was sitting inside the boot, very pleased with herself. After that, when Fig sat quiet under the spout, the others understood that he was keeping the minutes.

volumes.title: A Hole in the Bottom
volumes.text:
Tin rusts. Mrs. Dabble the water vole knew it, and still it was a shock, one wet June morning, to find a small brown hole in the floor of her kettle and the marsh coming up through it.

She was ashamed. She stuffed the hole with moss, put the lid down, and told callers that the tea house was closed for cleaning. It stayed closed five days, while the moss went soggy and the bed went damp.

It was the frogs, Plip and Plop, who peered down the spout and saw her bailing. Within the hour the whole marsh knew, and within two the whole marsh had come. Ripple the otter brought blue clay from the weir. Fig the newt remembered that pine pitch keeps water out. They patched it together, badly at first and then well. A trouble behind a closed lid, said Mrs. Dabble, only gets wetter.

volumes.title: Mrs. Coot Hears Something
volumes.text:
It began when Mrs. Dabble the water vole remarked, over the mint, that she was thinking of moving the lid. It stuck in wet weather, and she wanted it an inch to the left.

Mrs. Coot the moorhen caught the word "moving" and nothing else. By noon she had told the reeds that Mrs. Dabble was moving. By dusk the alder had it that the tin kettle was closing and its keeper leaving for the Lowlands, heartbroken, on account of the damp.

Next evening the whole marsh arrived with parting gifts: snail shells, a feather, and a speech from Ripple the otter that made him cry. Mrs. Dabble stood in her doorway holding a farewell beetle and understood nothing. It was Fig the newt who walked the story backwards, mouth by mouth, to one inch of lid. The gifts were kept. So was the speech, for a later date.

volumes.title: A Summer Without Rain
volumes.text:
No rain fell on the marsh below Emberwick for six weeks that summer. The river Ember shrank between its banks. The reeds stood in cracked mud, and the tin kettle, which had been at the water's edge, now sat a long hot walk from it. By noon the tin was too warm to touch.

Mrs. Dabble the water vole moved her tea to the evenings. But the lid was dry, the mint was limp, and Ripple the otter came back from the weir with an empty basket.

Grimsby the heron spoke, from his usual distance. He alone stood high enough to see over the reeds. "There is deep water under the third alder," he said, as if it bored him. "And green mint beside it. I have been standing in it all week." He led them there, stalking ahead, not once looking back to see whether they followed.

volumes.title: The Frogs Fall Out
volumes.text:
Plip and Plop, the two young frogs of the tin kettle, quarrelled in August over who should sit on the spout. Each said it had always been his place. By evening Plip was sulking on the east bank and Plop on the west, and each had told Mrs. Dabble the water vole that he would take his tea alone, thank you.

Mrs. Dabble said that was quite all right. She set out the tea as usual.

There was, as there had been since the first day, one acorn cup. She filled it and put it on the flat stone exactly halfway between them. The frogs looked at the cup, and at each other, and at the cup. Mint tea does not keep. Plip took a sip and, from long habit, passed it on. Plop drank and passed it back. Nobody sat on the spout that night.

volumes.title: Mending Day
volumes.text:
When the alder leaves begin to yellow, the creatures of the marsh get the tin kettle ready for winter. They have a day for it. Ripple the otter fetches fresh pitch for the patch in the floor. The frogs, Plip and Plop, pile dry reed over the top for thatch. Mrs. Coot the moorhen supervises, which is to say she talks.

That autumn Fig the newt, who rarely suggested anything, suggested a rope. The river Ember had brought the kettle, he said, and might one day wish to take it on.

So they plaited one out of rushes, sitting in a row along the bank. It was as thick as an otter's tail when they finished. Mrs. Dabble the water vole tied one end to the kettle's handle and the other round an alder root. Grimsby the heron watched from the shallows and said it would never hold.

volumes.title: The Night the Ember Rose
volumes.text:
The flood came in December, in the dark. Mrs. Dabble the water vole woke to find her tin kettle rocking, and the frogs and Fig the newt scrambling in through the lid, and the river Ember going by on every side, brown and loud.

The kettle floated. It swung out on its rush rope until the rope hummed. One strand parted, then another. Inside, four small creatures held on to each other and to the reed-fluff bed.

Then the swinging stopped. Something had taken hold of the handle. Mrs. Dabble looked up the spout and saw, against the racing clouds, a long grey neck bent right down to her roof. Grimsby the heron stood thigh-deep in the flood with the kettle's handle in his beak. He stood there until morning. He had said the rope would not hold, and he did not care to be proved right.

volumes.title: Tea on Higher Ground
volumes.text:
After the flood the creatures of the marsh rolled the tin kettle up the bank, a hand's breadth at a time, and set it under the alder, above the highest line of driftwood. Ripple the otter pushed. The frogs steered. Mrs. Coot the moorhen told everybody how.

Mrs. Dabble the water vole put the lid on straight, an inch to the left, and waited for a sunny day. It came. The mint was last summer's, dried, and the tea was the colour of pond water, and nobody minded.

She filled the acorn cup for the frogs to share. She set a second one on top of the kettle. Grimsby the heron came pacing up the bank, and bent his long neck, all the way down, until one yellow eye was level with her door. "Good evening," he said. The kettle has never once boiled. It has not needed to.

volumes.title: The Smallest Egg
volumes.text:
Once upon a wren, there was an egg. It lay with five others in a ball of moss tucked into the ivy on the old orchard wall at Emberwick, and it was the smallest of the six, no bigger than a hazelnut and speckled like a wall in the rain.

The other five hatched on a Monday. The sixth took until Wednesday, and when it finally cracked, what came out was mostly beak. Her mother named her Tuppence, on the grounds that she was not worth much more to look at.

A wren is the smallest bird in the orchard, and Tuppence was the smallest wren. Her brothers sat on her. The wind nearly had her out of the nest twice. But she opened that beak at the sky and made a noise that stopped a passing bee in mid-air. It was a start.

volumes.title: A Voice Too Big
volumes.text:
Tuppence the wren was three weeks old, the size of a walnut, and louder than the orchard gate. When she sang, her whole body shook with it and her tail stuck straight up.

Her brothers begged her to hush. Marlow the rook, who ruled the tall elms and liked his mornings dignified, flew down to say that small birds ought to make small noises. So Tuppence tried. For a whole day she whispered, and felt like a kettle with the lid held on.

That evening Marmalade the orchard cat came along the top of the wall, slow as honey, toward the ivy where the wren brood sat dozing. Tuppence saw her first. She forgot about whispering. The alarm she let out sent five wrens into the brambles, woke the rooks, and so startled Marmalade that she fell off the wall. Nobody asked for quiet again.

volumes.title: A Very Poor Rook
volumes.text:
Tuppence the wren admired the rooks. They were large and black and walked about the orchard at Emberwick as though they owned the grass. She decided to be one.

She puffed out every feather until she was nearly the size of a plum. She practised walking instead of hopping, and tripped. She tried to caw, and produced a squeak. Last of all she chose a stick for her nest, a proper rook's stick as long as a rake handle, and it pinned her to the ground until a kind beetle lifted the end.

Mrs. Dunnock, the brown hedge-bird who nested low in the quince, watched without laughing. "You make a very poor rook," she said. "Have you looked at the wall? There are forty cracks in it with a spider at the back of each. No rook alive can fit his beak in one." Tuppence looked. It was true.

volumes.title: Through the Gap
volumes.text:
Mrs. Dunnock's youngest fledgling went missing on a warm afternoon. He was found by his cheeping, deep inside the woodpile behind the orchard wall, where he had hopped after a woodlouse and could not find the way back.

The whole orchard came to help. Marlow the rook heaved at a log, and the pile shifted in a way nobody liked. Brisk the robin tried the gap and got as far as his shoulders. The cheeping grew smaller.

Tuppence the wren did not puff herself up. She pulled every feather flat and went in like a mouse, along a tunnel no wider than a thumb, round two corners in the dark. She came out backwards, scolding, with the fledgling hopping after the sound of her. Mrs. Dunnock said thank you eleven times. Marlow said nothing, but he looked at the gap for a long while.

volumes.title: The Robin's Line
volumes.text:
Brisk the robin had sung from the orchard wall at Emberwick for three summers, and he considered every stone of it his. When Tuppence the wren began singing from the same wall, he flew at her with his red chest out.

They held a shouting match. It lasted two days. He sang from the gatepost and she sang from the ivy, louder and louder, until both were hoarse and Marlow the rook complained from the elms that nobody could hear themselves think.

It was the hoarseness that settled it. Unable to shout, they were obliged to talk. Brisk, it turned out, wanted the top of the wall, the spade handles and the open ground where worms came up. Tuppence wanted the cracks, the ivy and the dark inside of things. They had been fighting over a wall that could be divided without cutting it anywhere.

volumes.title: The Cuckoo's Tall Tales
volumes.text:
A cuckoo rested in the orchard at Emberwick one July evening on her way south. She told Tuppence the wren about deserts, and rivers a mile wide, and trees full of fruit in January. She said a wall was a poor sort of world, and that only dull birds stayed.

Tuppence did not sleep. At dawn she set off after the cuckoo, flying low from hedge to hedge as wrens do, and by afternoon she had come farther than any wren of her family: to the cliffs of the Grey Coast, where the land simply stopped.

She sat on a gorse bush and looked at the sea. It was very large and had no cracks in it. She looked for an hour, glad to have seen it, and then she turned round. There is no shame in going to the edge of the map and deciding you prefer the middle.

volumes.title: The Knothole in the Hayloft
volumes.text:
In August the orchard at Emberwick was all plenty. There were spiders in every crack and flies on every plum, and Tuppence the wren grew round and idle.

Mrs. Dunnock tried to teach her the winter places: which stones kept beetles under them in frost, where the moss stayed soft. "You will want this," she said. Tuppence said yes, yes, and chased a moth instead. Winter was only a word the old birds used.

She did learn one thing that month, and it was not from prudence. She was simply nosy. High in the wall of the hayloft across the lane was a knothole the size of an acorn cup, and behind it a space lined with old hay, dry and still and smelling of summer. She went in, turned round, came out, and forgot about it until the nights turned cold.

volumes.title: Feathers on the Ground
volumes.text:
At summer's end Tuppence the wren began to fall apart. First one tail feather dropped out, then the other five. Her head came up in tufts. She looked, she thought, like something the cat had considered and declined.

She hid in the thickest part of the bramble by the orchard wall and resolved to stay there until spring. The bramble, she discovered, was already occupied. Far at the back, hunched and silent, sat Marlow the rook, lord of the elms. He was bald about the face, and one wing was showing its quills like a broken fan.

They looked at each other for some time. "It is called the moult," said Marlow at last, stiffly. "It happens to the best of us. I should be obliged if you did not mention it." They shared the bramble for a fortnight, and a great many blackberries, and neither has mentioned it since.

volumes.title: The First Cold Night
volumes.text:
The first frost came to the orchard at Emberwick in November, and Tuppence the wren met it alone. She had quarrelled with her five brothers in the summer over her singing, and had told them she could do very well without them.

By day this was true. By night it was not. A wren weighs about as much as a large coin, and so small a body cannot keep its warmth till morning. She tried the ivy, and the wind came through. She tried a crack in the wall, and the stone was like ice.

She sat with her feathers fluffed out and her feet tucked up and counted the hours. Across the orchard she could hear, faintly, other wrens settling down in other cold places, each one alone, each one too proud or too far away to say so. It was a long night, and she spent it thinking.

volumes.title: Nine in a Knothole
volumes.text:
On the second night of frost Tuppence the wren remembered the hayloft. She remembered the knothole high in its wall and the dry, hay-lined space behind it, which she had found in August out of pure nosiness.

There was room in it for more than one. So she sat on the hayloft roof at dusk and did the thing she was best at. She sang, with her tail straight up, loud enough to be heard from the orchard wall to the lane's end, and what the song said was: here, here, warm, here.

They came. Her five brothers came first, pretending they had been passing. Then three strangers arrived from the hedges. Nine wrens went through the knothole one after another and packed themselves into a ball, heads in and tails out. Tuppence was in the middle. It was the warmest she had ever been, and the quietest.

volumes.title: Snow and the Rook
volumes.text:
Snow lay a foot deep on the orchard at Emberwick, and the rooks were hungry. The ground they dug in was buried and frozen. Marlow, lord of the elms, sat on the hayloft roof with his feathers out and his dignity mostly gone.

Tuppence the wren came out of her knothole and saw him. She said nothing about the size of rooks. She went back inside, along the beam, and down to the hayloft floor, where the farmer's sacks had leaked oats into every gap between the boards.

One oat is a fair load for a wren. She carried it to the knothole and pushed it out, and it fell on the snow. Then she fetched another. By midday there was a small gold patch under the wall and seven rooks standing round it. Marlow ate last. Before he flew, he left one black feather on the sill.

volumes.title: A Nest of Her Own
volumes.text:
Spring came back to the orchard wall at Emberwick. A cock wren with a fine opinion of himself built three nests for Tuppence to choose from: one in the woodpile, one in the quince, and one in the ivy, in the very place where she had hatched.

She chose the ivy. She lined it herself, as wren hens do, with moss and hair, and with one black rook's feather that she had kept all winter. Brisk the robin sang from the top of the wall and left the cracks to her.

She laid six eggs. Five hatched on a Monday. The sixth, the smallest, took until Wednesday, and what came out was mostly beak. It opened that beak at the sky and made a noise that stopped a bee. Tuppence looked at it with great satisfaction. Once upon a wren, she thought, and tucked it under her wing.
